title: My final newsletter – fewer meetings, less management, slower pay growth?
gist: Resolution Foundation's weekly newsletter (final edition by the departing Deputy Chief Executive) covers meetings and wage growth, a fall in UK wellbeing, a summary of Paul Gregg's welfare essay, childcare subsidy fragmentation and, as chart of the week, rising earnings inequality in the 2026 ASHE data with low pay no longer falling.

insights.claim: The share of UK workers in low pay failed to fall for the first time in 15 years in the 2026 ONS Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: The long decline in low pay has stalled, relevant for consumer-spending distribution and minimum-wage politics.

insights.claim: UK overall earnings inequality (90:10 ratio) has ticked up across the board after a decade of decline, as the National Living Wage now only keeps pace with median pay and high earners pull away.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Minimum-wage compression of the pay distribution has ended; inequality now rising again.

insights.claim: Weekly pay at the 90th percentile grew 7.3 per cent nominal this year to 1,433 pounds a week, against 1.1 per cent at the 10th percentile.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: High-earner pay growth far outpaces low-end growth, supporting demand for premium goods and services relative to low-end consumers.

insights.claim: Among men, earnings inequality is at its joint-highest on record alongside 2014, as the 10th-percentile weekly pay fell in cash terms from 309 pounds in 2025 to 301 pounds in 2026.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Falling cash pay at the bottom signals acute low-end household squeeze.

insights.claim: Women's weekly earnings have long been less equal than men's because of higher part-time shares, but the genders have been slowly converging since the series began in 2002.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Part-time structure drives the gender gap in weekly inequality.

insights.claim: The number of out-of-work benefit recipients has risen by about 1.5 to 2 million since 2016 despite a stronger labour market, so alarm bells should have rung much earlier.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Structural welfare dependency growth is a persistent fiscal pressure.

insights.claim: Paul Gregg argues the 2000s-early 2010s combination of job-search conditionality, part-time work incentives, caseworker support and job placements worked, but support has since reverted to a cheaper sanction-based regime with in-work benefits cut back.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Indicates which policy levers have historically reduced claims.

insights.claim: The current UK Government does not appear to have a coherent strategy for reforming welfare into work, with its focus mainly on cost-cutting, though the imminent Milburn review may change that.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Expect savings-led, piecemeal welfare policy and fiscal-forecast risk.

insights.claim: Carnegie UK's Life in the UK index, based on about 6,700 people, put collective UK wellbeing at 61 out of 100, the first fall since the index began in 2023, with economic wellbeing down two points to 70 on cost-of-living pressures.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Subjective measures confirm persistent cost-of-living strain, a political risk factor.

insights.claim: Social renters score 25 points below homeowners on economic wellbeing (50 versus 75), and people aged 55+ score six points higher on wellbeing than younger groups.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Housing tenure and age are the main fault lines in UK wellbeing.

insights.claim: England has three childcare subsidy schemes run by different parts of government with different rules, and only two-fifths of Universal Credit families who pay for childcare claim the childcare element, while Tax-Free Childcare take-up is under half.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Low take-up means subsidy spend is below design and the sector's demand is dampened; consolidation could raise take-up.

insights.claim: A new report recommends a single childcare support system with subsidy rates that vary smoothly by income to prevent cliff-edges, a reform Resolution Foundation has also called for.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Possible Budget-adjacent policy direction affecting childcare providers and parents' work incentives.

insights.claim: Research on Norwegian workers finds the average worker spends 4.7 hours per week in meetings, more for managers, and more meeting time correlates with faster wage growth, with higher-paying firms meeting more.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Suggests coordination time is valued by firms rather than pure waste.
insights.locator: This could have been an email

insights.claim: An experiment with about 500 German students found selective memory fuels procrastination: those not reminded of bad workload news put the chance of light work 10 points higher, and each 10-point rise in hoped-for ease meant 7 per cent less work done early.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Behavioural evidence that reminders improve early task completion.

insights.claim: Chancellor Healey's first Budget is due the week after the newsletter, and Resolution Foundation will run an overnight analysis and a morning-after event.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: The Budget is the near-term UK fiscal catalyst to watch.
